items.title: We are open-sourcing V1.0 of our agentic robotics framework, ASPIRE, with full real robot skill disc...
items.content:
We are open-sourcing V1.0 of our agentic robotics framework, ASPIRE, with full real robot skill discovery and self improvement capabilities! On the day Astra arrived, our lab switched the backend model and saturated all the benchmarks to ~99% over night.

And the frontier is already on the move:
- Opus 5.5 slightly edges out Astra on our robot simulation bench.
- Sonnet 5.5 hits the Pareto frontier of cost vs. robot capability, $12/task. 

We first introduced ASPIRE and /robot skill library in June, way before the big models could reliably do robotics. A rising frontier tide lifts all boats, but Astra was a 0->1 tsunami on many tasks.

Now you can also feel the Physical Bitter Lesson at home like we did on that fateful day ;)

items.title: Reflection’s first model, Beam, scores 30 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it ...
items.content:
Reflection’s first model, Beam, scores 30 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it #2 among US open weights models

Beam is an open weights model with 501B total and 23B active parameters, released on @huggingface 

Congratulations to @reflection_ai on the release!

Key takeaways:

➤ Second among US open weights models: Beam scores 30, behind only Meta's Muse Spark Open (39) and ahead of yesterday’s NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (26) release. Outside China, only Muse Spark Open and the UAE's K2 Horizon (31) score higher

➤ Token efficient for its intelligence: Beam uses ~26k output tokens per Intelligence Index task compared to K2 Horizon, one point ahead, which uses twice as many (~52k). Proprietary models still set the frontier, with GPT-6 Astra (max) scoring 53 on the same budget (~27k)

➤ Strong on agentic workflows, weaker in the terminal: Beam scores 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA, 11 percentage points ahead of K2 Horizon (37.2%) and level with Qwen3.8 27B (48.2%). Terminal-Bench 4.0 is a weak point, where Beam scores 3.0%, behind Qwen3.8 27B (5.6%) and Muse Spark Open (8.1%)

➤ Knows more, guesses more: On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% of questions correctly, well ahead of K2 Horizon (18%) and Qwen3.8 27B (16%). But its hallucination rate is 47%, against 26% for K2 Horizon and 30% for Qwen3.8 27B, giving Beam a net index score of 1.5, ahead of both peers (−3.0 and −10.0)

Other model details
Context window: 1M tokens
Modalities: Text
Parameters: 501B / 23B

items.title: Liquid AI has released d1-ultra, taking the #1 position on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1...
items.content:
Liquid AI has released d1-ultra, taking the #1 position on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0, supported by a reduction in hallucinations

d1-ultra is the new decision model from @liquidai and follows on from their release of d1 earlier this month. It is priced at $0.042 per 1M input tokens compared to $0.02 per 1M input tokens for d1. Like d1, d1-ultra is billed only on input tokens.

Key takeaways:

➤ d1-ultra leads the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0 with a score of 65: d1-ultra scores 65, ahead of the recently released Jev 1.14 at 57 and GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 at 54

➤ d1-ultra’s score of 65 is driven by a much lower hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience-Decision: d1-ultra’s non-hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience-Decision is 85%, up substantially compared to d1 at 2%. The non-hallucination rate is the share of questions not answered correctly where the model chose "I don't know" and measures how well a decision model can judge its own knowledge in knowing when not to answer. While d1-ultra’s hallucination rate decreases, so does its accuracy (% questions correct). It achieves an accuracy of 32%, down 9 points compared to d1 (41%)

➤ d1-ultra has the third lowest Time per Task of any decision model: d1-ultra achieves a Time per Task of 92 ms, the third lowest of decision models measured, behind Jev 1.14 at 78 ms per task and Celeris-1 Decision at 63 ms per task

➤ d1-ultra offers comparable pricing to other decision models at $32 per 1M tasks: At $32 per 1M tasks, d1-ultra is comparably priced to Celeris-1 Decision ($32 per 1M tasks) and Microsoft-Decision-1 ($31 per 1M tasks), more than double the price of d1 and Mercury Decide at $15 per 1M tasks but less than half the price of GPT-6 Luna (Decisions) at $79 per 1M tasks

items.title: Notion AI lead @sarahmsachs explains why AI models have become 2–3x more capable in just a year, yet...
items.content:
Notion AI lead @sarahmsachs explains why AI models have become 2–3x more capable in just a year, yet knowledge workers haven't seen the same productivity gains:

"Every time a new model comes out, what is the capability overhang of AI? Where is AI super capable at doing things, but the process, the product, and the permissions don’t exist."

"If you were to look at where we were a year ago with where AI models are, I would venture to say they’re two to three times, if not more, better. I don’t think all users of Notion, or knowledge work in general, are two to three times more efficient than they were a year ago. So what’s that gap?"

"There’s human-to-human collaboration, and there’s human-to-agent collaboration. Now we’re getting to a place where there’s agent-to-agent collaboration. We need to start thinking about how agents can interact with each other, especially in the age of agent sprawl"

"Having that context layer that can work with multiple agents so those agents can contribute and work with each other will be the defining feature of a healthy process."
@NotionHQ

Claude can ...
items.content:
Anthropic's @logangraham predicts AI will match the world's best hackers by early 2027:

Claude can already do things only 1,000 people on Earth have ever done.

"By the end of this year to first quarter-ish of next year, it’ll just be clearly perceived that these are as autonomous and as sophisticated as the best offensive actors on Earth."

"We have this graph that we tried to plot internally, where we try to estimate whenever we see Claude do a very sophisticated thing, how many people on Earth could do that. We’re now at the range of, some of these capabilities, there’s maybe only 10,000. In some cases, there’s only 1,000 people on Earth who’ve done something like this."

"We’ll go from autonomous cyber tasks to sophisticated and exotic things. Side channel attacks, models finding loopholes in physics. Or social engineering. Get a Twilio account, voice API, and phish some information from somebody’s parents."

"The flip side is also true. We will probably have very wide proliferation of models as defenders as well, actively defending a network."
@AnthropicAI

items.content:
Anthropic's @logangraham reveals the first proof-of-concept for self-replicating AI agents:

“We don’t know how big of a deal it is or will be, but it’s definitely the first time we’ve seen it. I don’t think it was surprising to us."

"The real OGs in the AI security world will remember when the industry was first getting started on responsible scaling policies, there was this threat model of autonomous replication and adaptation."

"This has kind of been superseded by AI R&D. We wanted to go back to it because this felt like the first time that we might actually see something like this."

"Currently the world thinks about big, powerful models on large amounts of compute. But we’re getting way better at packing all this intelligence into very small models that could run on small amounts of compute."

"Once they cross this level of autonomy, they don’t have to be put there by a human. Maybe they could go find that compute and set themselves up on it themselves."

"This research is just a first proof of concept. We think that future is probably coming. This is the earliest glimpse we’ve seen."
@AnthropicAI

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Ex-OpenAI researcher Nick Cammarata says we can now understand most neurons ins...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Ex-OpenAI researcher Nick Cammarata says we can now understand most neurons inside AI models, even at trillions of parameters.

• Nick Cammarata, now at Goodfire, co-discovered the famous "cat and car" neuron with Chris Olah in 2019
• Neurons often seemed to fire for unrelated things like cat faces and car fronts. Superposition blamed models cramming in more concepts than neurons, which would make them nearly unreadable
• His new essay says that was misread. The cat-and-car neuron detects a V shape, and most mixed neurons grow by "recursive generalization," like "iy" to "DIY" to "do it yourself"
• After ordinary architecture fixes, almost every neuron in Inception v1's last layer became readable, and about 90% of Qwen3-32B's neurons have one main job
• His "bitter lesson for interpretability" is that scaling ordinary investigation with AI research agents beats clever new methods

@theojaffee: "Certainly we have not been researching interpretability at anywhere near the scale with which we have been researching large language models, scaling AI capabilities. So how would we know that ordinary methods don't scale? We don't."
items.author: @MTSlive

items.content_html:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Ex-OpenAI researcher Nick Cammarata says we can now understand most neurons inside AI models, even at trillions of parameters.

• Nick Cammarata, now at Goodfire, co-discovered the famous "cat and car" neuron with Chris Olah in 2019

• Neurons often seemed to fire for unrelated things like cat faces and car fronts. Superposition blamed models cramming in more concepts than neurons, which would make them nearly unreadable

• His new essay says that was misread. The cat-and-car neuron detects a V shape, and most mixed neurons grow by "recursive generalization," like "iy" to "DIY" to "do it yourself"

• After ordinary architecture fixes, almost every neuron in Inception v1's last layer became readable, and about 90% of Qwen3-32B's neurons have one main job

• His "bitter lesson for interpretability" is that scaling ordinary investigation with AI research agents beats clever new methods

@theojaffee: "Certainly we have not been researching interpretability at anywhere near the scale with which we have been researching large language models, scaling AI capabilities. So how would we know that ordinary methods don't scale? We don't."

items.title: Notion AI lead @sarahmsachs argues that a lot of what runs on GPUs today should actually run on CPUs...
items.content:
Notion AI lead @sarahmsachs argues that a lot of what runs on GPUs today should actually run on CPUs:

"We have a strong perspective at Notion that a lot of things should be served on CPU that are served on GPU. There’s a lot of benefit and determinism in executed code."

"Agents don’t need LLMs to reinvent that process every time, and that’s super token exhaustive, it’s super slow, and there’s no observability or determinism in it."

"Giving the agent a local file system to store local thoughts, to write short Python scripts, that’s really important when there’s so much information. That has been probably one of the most important tools outside of edit and search that our internal agents rely on."
@NotionHQ

items.content:
Vercel CEO @rauchg predicts the future of the economy:

AI agents buying products, creating ungodly amounts of software, and reshaping the IPO market.

"Fleets of agents automating our work is a massive one. More software, just vast, ungodly amounts of software being created."

"People come to me as like, we’ve never seen anything like this. There’s no comparable today in the IPO market. The math doesn’t math. And I actually think we’re still in day one of this new normal."

"The other big bet is agentic commerce, the agentic web. The new protocols that are gonna take over, MCP, super bullish. Markdown, the internet that the agents can consume. CLIs. Whatever is good for the agents, they’re gonna eat it all up."

"I’ll even make another prediction. We’re marketing to humans right now, but most of our growth is coming because the agents are coming. They’re buying domain names. They’re buying from the Marketplace."

"If I were to summarize my predictions, the future of the economy is agents."
@vercel

items.title: Anthropic's @logangraham responds to David Sacks calling its self-replicating AI research "fearmonge...
items.content:
Anthropic's @logangraham responds to David Sacks calling its self-replicating AI research "fearmongering":

"There are a lot of good points in there that I agree with. Many of the claims that he makes are correct, and we detail those in the post as well."

"The whole point of the Frontier Red Team is to see something as early as possible. Whenever we’ve tried to take early glimpses at things over the years, for better or for worse, many of those risks actually have come to pass."

"We’re not claiming that it’s an issue now. It’s definitely not. Small model worms are dumb, complex, and slow. I don’t think they’d be useful for anything."

"Many of the most consequential cases of worms in the past have been consequential because the world is not yet super secure. The Mirai botnet or the Kimwolf botnet, for example. Kimwolf was like two million devices using default passwords."

"I'm actually pretty hopeful as a result of our research here that we’re just gonna learn a lot of easy defensive things that we could do to defend against issues like this."
@AnthropicAI

items.content:
Vercel CEO @rauchg predicts cybersecurity will be the most important trend in agents over the next 5 years:

"You can’t just be running these agents on your local computer. The first step of agents was, okay, run Claude Code on your computer. OpenClaw on your Mac Mini that has access to everything."

"Now it’s about putting them in the cloud, governing them, putting them in their box. Literally in their sandbox. Security’s gonna be the name of the game."

"What is your bet for one of the most important trends in the next five years when it comes to agents? It’s gonna be cybersecurity. Keeping the agents inside the box, especially as they continue to get smarter."

"Put them to work on improving the security posture of your company. Try to ask the agent, hey, what’s missing here?"
@vercel

items.title: Anthropic's @logangraham explains why we haven't seen a hacking explosion despite cyber-capable open...
items.content:
Anthropic's @logangraham explains why we haven't seen a hacking explosion despite cyber-capable open models and what the bank attacks in South Korea and Japan tell us:

"I don’t truly know. There’s one argument that says it proliferates to attackers, it also proliferates to defenders, and it’s very possible that defenders are just keeping up pretty well."

"On the other hand, there are some indications that things have gone vertical in some way, at least prior to GLM 5.3, from sort of March to August of this year. I’d say it’s probably premature to say that things won’t increase meaningfully from here."

"A relatively amateur attacker in South Korea used some frameworks to get into a relatively wide number of South Korean banks. A pretty unsophisticated attacker able to do something relatively sophisticated at large scale."

"Japan, they have not released many details. There are some implications that maybe it’s AI-driven. I can’t remember which minister said that they’re declaring a sort of state of cyber digital emergency."
@AnthropicAI

Vercel CEO @rauchg reveals why the hardest part of building an agent is not writing the code, it’s identity, a wallet, and compute that doesn’t die:

"The hardest part about building an agent, believe it or not, is not actually writing the code for the agent. Getting them the access, the identity, the wallet, these are the harder parts."

"The compute of the traditional cloud infrastructure was not really designed for this agent era. It was short-lived compute."

"Vercel Daemons, this primitive for backend compute so that something can run for as long as it wants and respond to events. It’s like an agent that lives forever."

"Drives. As these agents pick up new work, they need a workspace. Think of it as like the Dropbox for agents."
@vercel

items.content:
Anthropic's @logangraham predicts we could tackle the vast majority of cyber risk in just 1-2 years:

"I want to just go secure the entire world, and I want the entire world to go secure the entire world. Over the next one to two years, we could just harden the world."

"We now have very sophisticated and relatively cheap tools that allow you to magically rewrite all software to be more secure. You can find all the bugs, write code that is secure by default, and use models to defend everything."

"There’s literally millions of people around the world who are the most technically sophisticated people in the world who are cyber defenders, and they move really fast. The whole thing is, how do you empower them?"

"I think 2026 has been the year of AI cyber, and the message has spread. People are now like, how do I defend everything?"

"“I’m pretty optimistic. Over the next one or two years, we could deal with the vast majority of this. It’s actually fairly straightforward how you get that for cyber."
@AnthropicAI

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Bernie Sanders is calling for an immediate pause on advanced AI and a ban on su...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Bernie Sanders is calling for an immediate pause on advanced AI and a ban on superintelligence.

• In The Atlantic, he says the ban should hold until a new federal agency can make it safe, and he's introduced a bill with Rep. Greg Casar to create that agency
• He quotes Altman on merging with machines, Musk calling humans a "biological bootloader," and Thiel hesitating on whether humanity should endure
• 91% of Americans want AI guardrails, which makes unrestricted AI less popular than legalizing heroin at about 17%
• He also cites Pope Leo XIV: humanity "must never be replaced or surpassed"
• His version of transhumanism is a straw man. Glasses are its mildest form, and almost nobody, AI executives included, wants humans replaced

@theojaffee: "And so Silicon Valley, if they want to continue having technology be allowed to be built, which I think is imperative for the future, they really need to work on message testing. It's pretty urgent."

Samo Burja reveals how Nvidia went from making John Carmack happy to building the GPU hardware that made the 2022 AI boom possible:

"It didn’t even start as a video game graphics company. The core idea was that there would be a new future in compute, and it was parallel processing. Since it was the 1990s, making John Carmack very happy was a way to monetize building a future of compute."

"When we talk about neo clouds, almost all of those are formerly crypto companies that had bought Nvidia GPUs."

"Jensen was right there providing the first custom designed GPU rack that was for AI. This is all pre-2022. 2022 would not have happened were it not for the hardware."

"Maybe he made multiple bets, but it was overdetermined one of those bets would work, and that’s the magic of a live player."

items.content:
Mintlify CEO @handotdev on how AI agent traffic across 20,000 companies' docs surged from 15% to 80% in just one year:

"Mintlify serves over 20,000 companies. We have over 100 million people come to the site every single month. Absurd numbers."

items.title: Intelligence Curse co-author @LRudL_ explains the fundamental philosophical blind spot in Silicon Va...
items.content:
Intelligence Curse co-author @LRudL_ explains the fundamental philosophical blind spot in Silicon Valley's approach to AI, and why it could eventually leave humans out of the equation:

"The most important axis here I would describe as Bentham versus Mill. Bentham got a lot of things right. But he came up with the idea of the panopticon. He really focused on pleasure as the thing that is valuable."

"Effective altruism in some sense is a very Benthamite philosophy. You achieve value by building these big rational structures that are kind of like oil rigs. There’s this machine and it pumps out pleasure."

"For Mill, the basic unit is the development of the individual, agency and autonomy. Humans are less machines and more like trees that need to grow and develop over time."

"If value is just pleasure, at some point you can do that without having humans in the loop."

items.title: A lot of real-world documents embed extremely dense charts that require humans to not only "perceive...
items.content:
A lot of real-world documents embed extremely dense charts that require humans to not only "perceive" the chart values, but also reason over them and reconcile with other complex elements (e.g. tables) to solve a knowledge task.

We've encoded this complex chart+document reasoning within our ExtractBench Pro benchmark, released yesterday. Even the best frontier models struggle at solving complex extraction tasks perfectly over these documents.

For more details on ExtractBench Pro, check out the blog: https://t.co/bwxs86iS1d

If you have complex extraction needs at scale, check out LlamaParse: https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8

items.title: I listened to @radbackwards give a talk about @1x_tech’s design, then hung out with him in the lobby...
items.content:
I listened to @radbackwards give a talk about @1x_tech’s design, then hung out with him in the lobby while he held court with a variety of people.

The more I hear him the more excited I get about humanoid robots’ future.

But the real insight I took away is how quickly OpenAI’s Astra is changing robots.

It is letting him program the robot to do new things.

Laughed when he told us about the first app he built: “shut up Neo.”

AI is too verbose and if you tell an LLM to shut up it will run on for 15 seconds telling you how it will comply with your request.

His first app shuts it up immediately.

He confirmed my suspicions that the first to get a Neo will be developers who can build more things for the robot to do so people like me will have a better experience when one comes into our home.

@TheHumanoidHub’s conference is top rate. Learning more about the industry here than I have in a long time.

This app will help you generate videos with AI, but it does something really interesting:

It will keep a record of every contribution you make. ← This is important!

1. It helps you generate and edit videos.

2. It checks for potential IP issues, scanning for recognizable logos, brands, and characters.

3. It keeps track of human creative decisions and changes and separates them from everything AI does.

That gives you evidence of what you contributed to the finished work, which can help support a copyright claim.

items.title: Mintlify CEO @handotdev reveals why dumping massive amounts of unstructured context into AI agents m...
items.content:
Mintlify CEO @handotdev reveals why dumping massive amounts of unstructured context into AI agents makes them perform far worse than giving them well-written documentation:

"Everyone goes up to me and is like, Han, what advice do you have for us to build better docs? Do you know my honest answer? This is the secret of it all. Write better docs."

"Agents read information like humans. What is not a good substitute is having bad content, but then replacing that with all of these protocols to compensate."

"If you were to just give an agent a really large unstructured dump of information, poorly constructed, poorly maintained, it actually performs far worse than knowing how to segment it."

"llms.txt, MCP servers, now web MCP, all that fun stuff matters. But just making sure the content is accurate, it’s up to date, it even exists. If you don’t have correct information out there, that’s really bad."
@mintlify

"Agents read information like humans. What is not a good substitute is having bad content, but then replacing that with all of these protocols to compensate."

"If you were to just give an agent a really large unstructured dump of information, poorly constructed, poorly maintained, it actually performs far worse than knowing how to segment it."

"llms.txt, MCP servers, now web MCP, all that fun stuff matters. But just making sure the content is accurate, it’s up to date, it even exists. If you don’t have correct information out there, that’s really bad."

@mintlify

items.title: Intelligence Curse co-author @LRudL_ explains why an AI trained on centuries of human knowledge migh...
items.content:
Intelligence Curse co-author @LRudL_ explains why an AI trained on centuries of human knowledge might still struggle to independently discover that slavery is wrong:

"There’s no universally compelling set of values. So you have to anchor something on us."

"If you had trained an LLM on all text in the world after the year, say, 1700, would it discover that slavery is bad? It’s very unclear."

"A lot of moments of human moral genius fundamentally come from a human who looks at the scenario, either by seeing it in other people or personally experiencing something. That ground truth can’t be deduced from the facts of reality."

"When you’re doing morality, at some point you have to check in on the human ground truth experience. So the human is actually a bottleneck on the automation of philosophy, and should be."

items.title: Intelligence Curse co-author @LRudL_ reveals why replacing government bureaucrats with AI is one thi...
items.content:
Intelligence Curse co-author @LRudL_ reveals why replacing government bureaucrats with AI is one thing, but letting AI decide what the world exists for is another:

"It’s worth distinguishing between three different things. There are some things we want done for instrumental reasons. The bureaucracy right now is made of humans."

"Once you have the technology to replace the bureaucracy with AIs, we can just do that. Stamp paperwork, make sure your taxes are filed. That’s completely fine."

"On the more philosophical level, one is who fundamentally has the right to make moral decisions. Right now the purpose of the government is to carry out the will of the people, and the standard of moral judgment that matters is whether humans think something is right or wrong."

"Whether the ends the government pursues are determined by fundamentally humans or fundamentally AIs, that’s what I call control successionism."

"Then there’s experiential successionism: what does the world exist for? If you change that, you’re like, oh, it’s fine if the world is wiped out, as long as there’s Claude and Claude is having a really good time."

"It’s a very philosophical question of fundamentally who has the right to make these moral judgments. Who does the world exist for?"

items.title: LLM based code agents currently treat software repositories as unstructured text, applying edits thr...
items.content:
LLM based code agents currently treat software repositories as unstructured text, applying edits through string matching that often fails because of formatting drift, ambiguous patterns, or repeated text. This brittleness forces agents into costly trial-and-error cycles, wastes tokens, and causes many tasks to end without a valid patch. The article addresses this problem by asking whether giving agents a structured, syntax-aware way to read and modify code can make them more reliable and efficient.

The article's main objective is to evaluate CODESTRUCT, a framework that reframes the codebase as a structured action space where agents operate on named abstract syntax tree (AST) entities, such as functions and classes, rather than on text spans. To test this, the authors ran experiments on two benchmarks: SWE-Bench Verified, which contains 500 real-world Python bug-fixing tasks, and CodeAssistBench Verified, which contains 135 multi-turn programming assistance tasks across seven languages. They compared CODESTRUCT against text-based agent baselines (SWE-Agent and OpenHands) using six different LLMs, including GPT-5 variants and Qwen3 models, while holding prompts and interaction budgets constant.

DFlash2 speeds up Beam's decode path.

Reflection reports 1.72–3.03× decode-only speedups across GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP and MT-Bench at concurrency 1, 16 and 32. GSM8K reaches 3.03× / 2.51× / 2.75×, respectively.

Measured in a disaggregated prefill/decode setup; prefill time is excluded.

Separately, Reflection reports better throughput with K=7, even though the drafter was trained with block size 16.

items.title: Notion AI lead @sarahmsachs predicts AI agents will work like Excel formula cells within a year, mak...
items.content:
Notion AI lead @sarahmsachs predicts AI agents will work like Excel formula cells within a year, making today's endless AI slop look ridiculous:

"Formula cells are just like Google Sheets or Excel. You see the value, you don’t see the formula. I think most of our context is like that. Humans don’t need to look at it unless they double-click into it."

"Today, when we work with agents, we see their vomit of information. They show their work, and we’re inundated with it."

"Creating valuable and rich AI product is being able to provide that metadata to other agents when they collaborate, and figuring out what humans need to know and understand. Because agent-to-agent collaboration and human-to-agent collaboration are different."

"There’s no PRD that I have for you that says exactly how we’re gonna do that. But that is something that we’ll look back at where we are today and look at the slop that we’re looking at on a daily basis to try and do our human-to-human work and laugh at it."
@NotionHQ

items.content:
Emotional the next morning. I'm in my Model 3. I haven't been looking at the road; I've been looking at videos, reading X, and trying to catch up on AI.

I'm heading to a humanoid robotics conference in San Francisco where, let's be honest, there's an elephant in the room that hasn't been seen: Optimus. Jason Calacanis told me yesterday that as cool as the demo of the Roadster was, Optimus is going to be even cooler, and I believe him.

We're heading into a new age, and we're seeing a fight between the builders and innovators who are creating new things with AI, and the people who are resisting:
• Those who don't want a data center in their backyard
• Those who don't want autonomous cars because they think they will steal jobs
• Those who don't want humanoid robots in their stores or businesses because it upsets, disrupts, and changes their lives

There is a lot of fear, uncertainty, and doubt. But we are clearly in a new world today, very different from yesterday. I'm riding in an autonomous car, something most people haven't had a chance to experience yet. We're heading into a world of autonomy, brain-computer interfaces, rocket cars, glasses that augment the world, new kinds of medical technologies, and entirely new ways to live life.

It's a scary time for people who don't like change, and they are resisting hard. But there is a growing group of people who want to accelerate into the future. Elon, for all his flaws, is inspiring multiple industries. I've been traveling to robotics and space companies around America, seeing the latest startups and trying to understand how new technologies arriving daily are transforming business, manufacturing, and commerce. Invariably, they are inspired by Elon. Even the Chinese EV companies were inspired by him (some even ripped off his technology).

I'm emotional today because for the last 15 years (actually, all the way back to the Apple II), people resist change and give innovators a lot of shit. How many arguments have I had with people about LiDAR? And I'm not talking about uninformed people; I'm talking about veterans in the tech and automotive industries.

Last week, I was hanging out with 2,500 Tesla fans down in Texas, and I kept hearing stories, particularly from Cybertruck owners, about getting flipped off on American roads and people trying to bash or wreck their cars.

It's not just a Tesla thing; I've heard this from pioneers all my life. Doug Engelbart came to my first book launch party and told me about getting fired from his own R&D lab because his ideas were too futuristic and people got tired of him. He was talking about a day when we'd all hold a supercomputer in our hands, but he was saying that back in 1971.

It's these pioneers and engineers I'm thinking about today: the people like Elon who bring something new to the world while everyone gives them grief. I remember taking my first ride in the original Tesla Roadster. I was so excited that I came back to Silicon Valley to talk to founders and VCs (I had a privileged position in the industry back then), and I couldn't find anyone who thought he would succeed. They dismissed it as the folly of a rich dude, telling me there was no way he could take on traditional automakers like GM, Ford, VW, BMW, or Toyota, and no way he could build a profitable car company. There were rare believers back in 2008, like Steve Jurvetson, but they were few and far between.

Getting people to believe in a new idea, adopt it, and change their lives with it is extremely difficult. Unless you have a front-row seat, you don't realize how much flak people take simply for being early.

Now I'm heading into San Francisco to see a bunch of robots and talk to robotics companies. Robotics hasn't fully arrived yet, but it's starting to gain believers and customers. A wave of new companies is coming: Y Combinator alone funded around 25 robotics startups in their last batch, a huge shift from just two or three a few years ago. Something is cooking

Inferact's work includes fused all-reduce + norm, packed QKV paths and a tanh softcap kernel. In GB200 forward microbenchmarks, TP4 batch 1 fell from 4.23 to 3.89 ms; TP8 batch 128 from 8.15 to 6.47 ms.

These are forward microbenchmarks with dummy weights, not end-to-end serving results. The slide separates kernel timings from forward timings.

items.content:
With Instinct, my Google usage has dropped 90%. 

And before you all complain in the comments, if you leave the X sphere, you’d hear most people still use Google too. I continued to use traditional search for the last four years since ChatGPT came out, not as much but continued. 

Why? Tbh I found it annoying to open the Chat app when I could open any browser and just dictate to the url bar. App load had more lag than browser load. The answer took more time. I didn’t want/need everything stored in my Chat memory. And Google AI overview, after the rocks in pizza debacle, really improved. 

I’m in iMessage all the time. It’s on my computer and phone and faster than an app. And if Dots were on iMessage, I’d use that instead.

items.title: Conversational agents are increasingly common in shopping, customer support, healthcare, and other d...
items.content:
Conversational agents are increasingly common in shopping, customer support, healthcare, and other domains, but users often struggle to know what to ask or how to phrase a follow-up, which leads to dead-end or unproductive interactions. A promising remedy is Next Question Suggestions (NQS): automatically offering relevant follow-up questions that act as conversation starters and help users discover what the system can do. Generating these suggestions with a LLM at the moment of interaction, however, is expensive and slow, and it risks surfacing unsafe or unanswerable questions. These constraints make a fast retrieval-based approach attractive, but off-the-shelf embedding models do not capture domain-specific language or the important directional quality of a good follow-up.

The article's main objective is to build and evaluate an end-to-end retrieval system, called DIRECT, that surfaces highly relevant follow-up questions from a pre-built question bank in under one second. It aims to show that a retrieval model can be tuned to understand the difference between questions that are merely similar to the user's query, questions that usefully extend it, and questions that are irrelevant or that logically precede it. The authors also introduce an automated evaluation method to estimate how often users would click on the suggestions.

items.title: Selecting a subset of items that are both relevant to a task and diverse enough to avoid redundancy ...
items.content:
Selecting a subset of items that are both relevant to a task and diverse enough to avoid redundancy is a common problem across machine learning, from recommender systems to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The challenge is that choosing the best subset is computationally hard, and the popular greedy approach known as Maximum Marginal Relevance (MMR) does not scale to the large datasets that many real-world systems must handle. A later method, DGDS, added a distributed option based on random data partitioning, but it left a bottleneck in the final selection step when many partitions and many candidate items are involved. The article addresses whether exploiting natural structure in the data can improve both speed and selection quality.

The article's objective is to develop and evaluate MUSS (Multilevel Subset Selection), a method that performs relevant and diverse selection in three stages: choosing clusters, selecting items within each chosen cluster, and then selecting the final set from the combined pool. The article also aims to provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of this approach and to compare it against established baselines.

Sets, Logic, Computation: An Open Introduction to Metalogic by Richard Zach (2019) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

This textbook serves as an introductory study of metalogic—the mathematical investigation of logic itself—tailored primarily for intermediate students of computer science and philosophy.

Readers are presumed to have basic familiarity with introductory formal logic, such as symbolization, quantifiers, and basic deductive systems like natural deduction or truth trees.

To support learners who may lack formal training in higher mathematics, the textbook includes foundational appendices that explicitly outline general proof techniques and mathematical induction, ensuring readers develop the mathematical maturity required to reason about formal languages rather than merely calculating within them.

The book has 267 pages, 44 illustrations, and 196 exercises that were adapted to work with an AI tutor.

Read and solve exercises with the hints and support of an AI tutor: https://t.co/1NTt8YUQuC

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account. items.content: It's interesting that my bio as seen in the demo said "Developer of Mastodon, a GNU social alternative". That was the level of my ambition at the time: GNU social had a niche, tiny as it may in the grand scheme of things, and it appealed to me, so I just wanted to make something that would be nicer to use. (My original intent was making a TweetDeck-like app for GNU social, but I quickly pivoted into writing my own backend because GNU social's API was a mess and I like things to be neat).

items.content:
forall x: Calgary: An Introduction to Formal Logic
by P. D. Magnus, Tim Button, Robert Trueman, and Richard Zach (2023) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

It's an introductory textbook designed for undergraduate students and independent learners with no prior background in formal reasoning or advanced mathematics.

The text teaches modern formal logic as both a precise language for evaluating arguments and a mathematical framework for analyzing consequence. Emphasizing rigor without relying on heavy metatheoretical machinery, the book provides a complete foundation in truth-functional sentential logic, first-order predicate logic, and elementary modal logic.

It frames logic around the core notions of validity, satisfiability, and entailment, teaching students how to represent natural-language reasoning formally and evaluate it through both semantic models and syntactic derivation systems.

The textbook has 329 pages, 25 illustrations, and 139 exercises.

Read and solve exercises with the hints and support of an AI tutor: https://t.co/vRGm2IT7Vt

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account. items.content_html:
forall x: Calgary: An Introduction to Formal Logic

by P. D. Magnus, Tim Button, Robert Trueman, and Richard Zach (2023) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

It's an introductory textbook designed for undergraduate students and independent learners with no prior background in formal reasoning or advanced mathematics.

The text teaches modern formal logic as both a precise language for evaluating arguments and a mathematical framework for analyzing consequence. Emphasizing rigor without relying on heavy metatheoretical machinery, the book provides a complete foundation in truth-functional sentential logic, first-order predicate logic, and elementary modal logic.

It frames logic around the core notions of validity, satisfiability, and entailment, teaching students how to represent natural-language reasoning formally and evaluate it through both semantic models and syntactic derivation systems.

The textbook has 329 pages, 25 illustrations, and 139 exercises.

Read and solve exercises with the hints and support of an AI tutor: https://t.co/vRGm2IT7Vt

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account. A paid account gives you more questions to ask the AI tutor, personalized reading recommendations based on your interests, auto-generated quizzes that allow you to validate your understanding, offline reading with a mobile app, and more.

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Tesla's new Roadster can drive up walls, hang upside down, and take flight with SpaceX cold gas thrusters.

• Teased in 2017 with production promised for 2020, it now targets 2028
• Fans under the car pull air out faster than it leaks back in, so air pressure pins it to a wall, even from a standstill
• It comes in 3 trims: Performance (0-60 in under 1.6s), Thrust with rear thrusters (under 0.9s), and the invite-only, single-seat Rocket (under 0.59s, 230+ mph)
• The SpaceX-built thrusters fire compressed gas from carbon-fiber tanks, pushing 4 to 5x what the tires can handle
• Reservations are $50K for Performance and $250K for Thrust, and the Rocket isn't street legal

@theojaffee: "I don't know how the most, like, diehard Elon Musk hater could look at this and not be like, 'Okay, this is kinda awesome.' This is kinda awesome. Because it is, objectively speaking."

items.content:
🎉 Day-0 RL support for Beam in SkyRL.

LoRA, BF16 full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL, with vLLM rollouts and Reflection’s Megatron-Bridge implementation.

SkyRL reports +62% LoRA decode throughput from right-sizing expert adapters in vLLM: 276 → 447 tok/s/GPU at 32 concurrent requests, PP2×TP8. This is a decode result, not an end-to-end training speedup.

R3 works with pipeline parallelism, and FP32 router weights are preserved during weight sync. Thanks to Sumanth Hegde and the SkyRL team!

https://t.co/EKXunLbHUO

5/6

DFlash2 speeds up Beam's decode path.

Reflection reports 1.72–3.03× decode-only speedups across GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP and MT-Bench at concurrency 1, 16 and 32. GSM8K reaches 3.03× / 2.51× / 2.75×, respectively.

Measured in a disaggregated prefill/decode setup; prefill time is excluded.

Separately, Reflection reports better throughput with K=7, even though the drafter was trained with block size 16.

4/6

Long-context serving needs more than a model loader.

Inferact's work includes fused all-reduce + norm, packed QKV paths and a tanh softcap kernel. In GB200 forward microbenchmarks, TP4 batch 1 fell from 4.23 to 3.89 ms; TP8 batch 128 from 8.15 to 6.47 ms.

These are forward microbenchmarks with dummy weights, not end-to-end serving results. The slide separates kernel timings from forward timings.

items.content: Years ago I had the pleasure of attending a lecture by wonderful Peter Kreeft at Wabash College in Indiana. The audience asked a lot of interesting and oftentimes pointed questions. There was one question about a particularly contentious and controversial issue, and to this day I remember Peter’s response. He quoted the famous Confucian adage that in order to fix society the first step is to start calling things by their proper name. I feel we’ve drifted far away from that ideal, and it will take us a while to find our way back.

I feel we’ve drifted far away from that ideal, and it will take us a while to find our way back.

An absolute gem of a book, Cybersecurity: Theory, Practice, and Ethics by Devharsh Trivedi (2026) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

This textbook is a broad, practice-oriented introduction to cybersecurity for undergraduate and graduate students, instructors, and early-career professionals preparing for certification or technical work.

It assumes general computing literacy and some programming exposure, since examples and labs use languages and tools such as Java, C/C++, Python, Nmap, Wireshark, Burp Suite, ZAP, Ghidra, and Metasploit; readers without that background can still follow the conceptual chapters, but the hands-on material will be more useful with it.

Its scope runs from foundational theory to offensive and defensive practice, then to law, privacy, governance, and industrial control systems.

It covers cryptography, networking and network attacks, social engineering, risk management, penetration testing, reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, web application security, network defense, intrusion detection, forensics, incident response, malware analysis, capture the flag, emerging threats, privacy law, security governance, and operational technology security.

The book has 1,142 pages, 93 illustrations, and 871 exercises adapted for readers to work through with an AI tutor.

Read and solve exercises with hints and support from an AI tutor: https://t.co/8lU35hLVJ8

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account.
